t: Aim and plan of the session
n: The aim of this session is to familiarise students with the toxicological significance and the methods of analysis of antidepressants such as amitriptyline, venlafaxine, mirtazapine and fluoxetine. The plan has two parts: the first is the toxicological significance of antidepressant drugs, the second is their methods of analysis. Title of the session: detection of antidepressant drugs in isolates and liquid physical evidence. The analysis is carried out by the TDSIS method, thermal desorption surface ionisation spectroscopy, and the quantitative analysis is carried out by the PEC method, that is photoelectrocolorimetry.

By the end of the session, students master the conditions for carrying out qualitative reactions in pure solutions of antidepressant drugs and in a solution of unknown composition. Items needed for the work: test tubes, separating funnels, reagents and visual aids. As for laboratory equipment, the session is held in a room equipped with special laboratory facilities.

About safety and preparation. For the laboratory work the student brings rubber gloves, a wipe and a face mask. The examination is carried out in rooms with ventilation and a fume cupboard, which are locked and sealed when the work is finished. Objects from infected persons, that is those with tuberculosis, hepatitis and AIDS, arrive in a special container and are noted in the documents.

Antidepressants are psychotropic drugs used in the treatment of depression. They improve mood, raise mental activity, and normalise sleep and appetite. In the table they are divided into generations. The first generation is tricyclic: imipramine 1957, amitriptyline. The second generation is heterocyclic: trazodone, mianserin. The third generation is the selective reuptake inhibitors.

By clinical action, antidepressants are divided into three groups. Sedative antidepressants are used in apathy and depressive agitation; examples: trimipramine, doxepin, amitriptyline. Stimulants are used in apathetic states; examples: imipramine, desipramine, nortriptyline. Balancing antidepressants are used in both cases; examples: maprotiline, sertraline, venlafaxine.

Now the toxicological significance. Signs of poisoning: dizziness, headache, urinary retention, constipation, dry mouth, blurred vision. In addition, skin rashes, euphoria, insomnia, hallucinations and mental disorders occur. Amitriptyline is significant both for its medical use and for its consumption as an intoxicant by toxicomaniacs. It potentiates the action of narcotic, psychotropic and hypnotic substances and prolongs the duration of action.

It is convenient to divide the signs of poisoning into four groups. In the central nervous system, dizziness, headache, euphoria and insomnia are observed. In the urinary and intestinal sphere, urinary retention and constipation occur. In the mouth and vision, dry mouth and blurred vision are found. In the skin and psyche, skin rashes, hallucinations and mental disorders may appear.

Amitriptyline is a tricyclic antidepressant, with the chemical name 10-11-dihydro-N,N-dimethyl-5-N-dibenzo-heptalene-propylamine. It is a cholinolytically active substance. Therefore in the body it can cause effects such as dry mouth, dilation of the pupil and urinary retention. In the treatment of alcoholic psychoses, up to 200-300 mg is recommended.

About metabolism. Amitriptyline is rapidly metabolised in the liver: N-demethylation, hydroxylation and conjugation with glucuronic acid take place. 60-70% is excreted in the urine, and about 5-10% is excreted unchanged in the urine. In choosing the object, urine is taken for screening. In severe poisoning or death, blood is analysed, because there is little poison in the urine.

Once more, pay attention to the figures. Antidepressants are rapidly metabolised in the liver, and 60-70% is excreted in the urine. About 5-10% is excreted unchanged in the urine. In the treatment of alcoholic psychoses, amitriptyline is recommended up to 200-300 mg. Remember: the unchanged part in the urine is small, so in severe poisoning blood is examined.

t: Isolating amitriptyline from blood and urine
n: Procedure for isolating amitriptyline from blood and urine. 5 ml of blood or 50 ml of urine is brought to pH=9-10 with 50% sodium hydroxide. Then it is extracted twice with 20 ml of ethyl ether, and the ether solution is made up to the mark in a 50 ml flask. The solution is divided into 4 portions of 10, 10, 10 and 20 ml and dried in porcelain dishes to a dry residue.

t: Isolating amitriptyline: volume and pH figures
n: Let us repeat the volume and pH figures of the isolation stage one by one. Blood 5 ml, urine 50 ml is taken. Extraction is carried out at pH=9-10. Ether is used twice, 20 ml each time. The volumetric flask is 50 ml. The ether isolates are made up to the mark in the flask and divided into portions of 10, 10, 10 and 20 ml.

t: From isolation to GC and HPLC
n: The route from isolation to gas chromatography and HPLC, that is high-performance liquid chromatography. The sample, that is blood or urine, is extracted in an alkaline medium with an organic solvent such as n-hexane. Then the organic layer is extracted with an acidic solution and determined by HPLC. Or it is re-extracted into an organic solvent and determined by gas chromatography.

Chromatographic purification and analysis are carried out on a Silufol plate. Concentrated sulphuric acid is used as the confirmatory reagent. See the table. In the first run, the benzene-acetone (80:20) system, 10 cm. In the second run, benzene-dioxane-ammonia (60:35:5), 10 cm. The spots are developed with concentrated H2SO4. Chloroform is used for dissolving, 3 times 10 ml.

The first stage of TLC. The dry residue is dissolved in chloroform and applied to the Silufol start line as a band 1-2 cm wide. Beside it, 5-10 drops of a 0.5 mg/ml chloroform solution of amitriptyline and nortriptyline bases are applied. The plate is first kept in the benzene-acetone (80:20) system until it rises 10 cm, then dried.

t: TLC: second run and developing the spots
n: In the second run, the plate is chromatographed a second time in a chamber with benzene-dioxane-ammonia (60:35:5) to 10 cm. The spots are developed with concentrated H2SO4. The Rf value of amitriptyline is 0.74-0.78, with a yellowish spot. The Rf value of nortriptyline is 0.38-0.46, with a pale yellowish spot. The detection limit for amitriptyline and nortriptyline bases is 0.3 µg.

Distinguishing amitriptyline from nortriptyline. Amitriptyline forms a clear ochre-coloured spot with Rf=0.74-0.78. Nortriptyline gives a yellow spot with Rf=0.38-0.46. With Reinecke salt, amitriptyline forms needle-like crystals, while nortriptyline forms antler-shaped crystals. So Rf, spot colour and crystal shape together make it possible to distinguish the two substances.

Recovering the spot. The part corresponding to the spot is scraped off with a scalpel and transferred to a stoppered test tube. It is shaken thoroughly three times with 10 ml of chloroform and the chloroform isolate is filtered. This isolate is used for the reactions with concentrated acids and Reinecke salt.

Reaction with concentrated acids. 20 ml of solution is evaporated until 3 ml of chloroform remains; a few drops are applied to each of three porcelain dishes. After the solvent has evaporated, two drops each of concentrated H2SO4, Fröhde reagent and Marquis reagent are added to the residue. A dark orange colour forms with all three reagents. If both substances are present, a dark orange colour appears; the sensitivity of the reaction is from 0.1 to 1.0 µg.

t: Scheme of the reaction with Mandelin reagent
n: Reaction with Mandelin reagent. Under the action of Mandelin reagent, a brown and then a green substance forms. Concentrated H2SO4, and Marquis and Fröhde reagents, give an ochre colour. The scheme shows that the amitriptyline residue reacts with Mandelin reagent and forms a coloured product.

Microcrystalloscopy with Reinecke salt. The last 10 ml chloroform isolate is evaporated on a microscope slide to a dry residue. To it, 1 drop of 0.1% HCl and 1 drop of 0.1% Reinecke salt solution are applied, and it is then examined under the microscope. Amitriptyline gives a cluster of needle-like crystals, and nortriptyline gives leaf-shaped microcrystals. The sensitivity in both cases is 0.2 µg.

Analysis of imizine, that is imipramine, is given for the qualification work. If concentrated nitric acid acts on the residue from an alkaline extract of imizine, a blue colour forms. If a drop of picric acid is applied to the residue, a yellow precipitate forms; characteristic microcrystals are seen under the microscope. In TLC on a KSK plate, a water-saturated chloroform system is used, Dragendorff reagent gives a brown spot, and the UV maximum in 0.01 M HCl is 251 nm.

Main indicators of fluoxetine. Fluoxetine is an antidepressant with basic properties, with a molecular mass of 345.8. It is a white crystalline powder; it dissolves in methanol at 250 mg/ml and in chloroform at 125 mg/ml, and also dissolves in acetone. Melting point 157.5-158.7 °C. It dissolves poorly in water, at most up to 14 g/l at 25 °C.

Let us compare venlafaxine and mirtazapine. Venlafaxine has the formula C17H27NO2, a molecular mass of 277.4, and basic properties. Mirtazapine has the formula C17H19N3 and a molecular mass of 265.3. Mirtazapine melts at 114-116 °C; its solution in 96% alcohol absorbs strongly at 295 nm. In TLC with Dragendorff reagent, mirtazapine gives a brown spot, Rf=0.42.

t: Isolating diphenhydramine from blood and urine
n: Isolating diphenhydramine from blood and urine. 10 ml of urine or 2 ml of blood is brought to pH=10 with ammonia and extracted twice with chloroform. For gas chromatography, the organic solvent is evaporated to a small residue. For quantitative analysis it is evaporated to a dry residue.

TLC systems are given for four antidepressants. For paroxetine, benzene-dioxane-25% ammonia in the ratio 60:35:5. For Depres, ethyl alcohol-chloroform-benzene in the ratio 2:1:2. For mirtazapine, ethyl acetate-methanol-water-ammonia in the ratio 87:3:1.5:0.5. For venlafaxine, ethyl acetate-ethyl alcohol-ammonia in the ratio 8.5:1:0.5. UV light, and Dragendorff and Mandelin reagents, are used as visualising reagents.

Let us compare gas chromatography and HPLC. In gas chromatography, the amount of tricyclic antidepressants is determined on capillary columns; the drawback is the need for derivatisation with trifluoroacetic anhydride. In HPLC, a C8 and C18 sorbent, a UV detector at 254 nm and an acetonitrile/methanol mobile phase are used. By HPLC, trimipramine, doxepin, amitriptyline, imipramine, nortriptyline and others are separated.

Steps of the TOXI-TUBES-A method. 5 ml of urine, or 2.5 ml of blood and 2.5 ml of water, is placed in a TOXI-TUBES-A tube and shaken for 5 minutes. To break the emulsion it is centrifuged at 3000 rpm. The organic layer is evaporated, the dry residue is dissolved in 1 ml of alcohol and analysed by TLC.

Diphenhydramine: TLC and UV spectrum. On a Silufol plate the chloroform-acetone-ammonia (12:24:1) system is used until it rises 10 cm; the developer is concentrated H2SO4. Diphenhydramine gives a yellow spot, Rf 0.58-0.60. Its metabolite benzhydrol forms a spot with Rf=0.76-0.80. In the UV spectrum, the solution in 0.1 M sulphuric acid absorbs at a maximum at 252 and 257 nm.

Colour reactions of diphenhydramine. The reagent is applied to the residue, with results in the table. Concentrated H2SO4 gives yellow, then red-brick. A mixture of H2SO4 and HNO3 gives red, Marquis reagent lemon yellow, and Liebermann reagent orange. The coloured complex formed with sulphuric acid breaks down when a few drops of water are added, and the colour disappears. If chloroform is added to the H2SO4+HNO3 product with added water and shaken, the chloroform layer turns violet.

t: The essence of PEC and quantifying diphenhydramine
n: The essence of PEC. Photocolorimetry is based on analysing a substance by measuring it in the visible part of the spectrum under polychromatic radiation. The quantitative analysis of diphenhydramine is based on the stable colour formed with the indicator acid chromotrope blue, which is stable in an acidic medium. For the standard scale, a chloroform extract containing diphenhydramine in the range of 0.05-0.3 mg is used.

Procedure for the PEC of diphenhydramine. The dry residue is dissolved in 1 ml of 0.1 M HCl, 10 ml of chloroform is added, and it is transferred to a measuring tube. Then 6.4 ml of acid chromotrope blue, that is 2.63 g of indicator in 1 l of water, is added, made up to 20 ml with water and shaken for 3 minutes. The absorbance of the chloroform layer is measured at 567 nm in a 10 mm cuvette.

t: The essence of the TDSIS method
n: The essence of the TDSIS method. Thermal desorption surface ionisation spectroscopy makes it possible to determine small residues of low-volatility active nitrogen-containing compounds. The molecules of the substance are vaporised in a programmed way and recorded on a surface ionisation detector, SID, in the form of a thermal desorption spectrum. The anode of the detector is a heated emitter, and the cathode is a collector of positive ions. Detection is carried out by effective desorption temperatures; the spectrum is compared with a reference spectrum from a computer data bank.

TDSIS analysis consists of seven stages. First, preparing the surface ionisation indicator PII-N-S Iskovich-1 for analysis; second, preparing the sample solutions. Third, applying the sample solution to the evaporator ribbon; fourth, carrying out the TDSIS analysis. Fifth, obtaining the thermal desorption spectra and saving them in the computer data bank. Sixth, comparing the obtained spectra with the reference spectrum; seventh, interpreting and recording the results.

TDSIS conditions for sertraline. The PII-N-S Iskovich-1 is a recommendation of staff of the U. A. Arifov Institute of Electronics of the Academy of Sciences of the Republic of Uzbekistan. The emitter is oxidised molybdenum with an iridium admixture, voltage 405 V, temperature 390-420 °C. Vaporisation from room temperature to 505 °C; air flow 50 l/hour; sample 1.0 µl; the analysis lasts 3 minutes.

The sertraline spectrum. Working standard solutions of sertraline of 50 µg/ml, 100 µg/ml and 200 µg/ml are prepared. With a microsyringe, 1 µl each is placed in the cylindrical well on the ribbon and the spectrum is obtained. Line peaks characteristic of sertraline appear at ~131±15 °C and ~190±15 °C.

Case 23 and the Snowstorm method. Condition of the case: patient T was poisoned by taking an excess of an antidepressant; carry out the forensic chemical analysis. Students are divided into 3 small groups; the group giving the correct answer is rewarded. The first group considers isolation and toxicological significance. The second group considers metabolites and amitriptyline by TDSIS. The third group carries out chromatographic analysis and authenticity analysis.

Interpreting the result and limitations. The formation of a spot in the ranges Rf=0.74-0.78 and Rf=0.38-0.46 gives direction for continuing the further analysis. The detection limit in TLC is 0.3 µg; the sensitivity of the colour reaction is 0.1-1.0 µg; the Reinecke reaction 0.2 µg. In TDSIS, the authenticity of the substance is assessed by comparing the spectrum with the reference spectrum.

Review questions. First: the toxicological significance and classification of antidepressant drugs; the toxicological and narcological significance of amitriptyline, its formula. Second: how is amitriptyline isolated from urine, which substance is its main metabolite, how is it determined by TLC, how is its amount determined? Third: isolation of diphenhydramine from urine and methods of analysis; the essence of the TDSIS method.

Conclusion. Amitriptyline: isolation with ether at pH=9-10, Silufol TLC, Rf=0.74-0.78, colours with Fröhde and Marquis reagents, Reinecke crystals. Diphenhydramine: isolation with chloroform at pH=10, in TLC Rf 0.58-0.60, PEC at 567 nm. TDSIS: 7 stages, for sertraline peaks at ~131±15 and ~190±15 °C.
